A STACK IS A DATA STRUCTURE THAT OPERATES ON THE LIFO (LAST-IN, FIRST-OUT) PRINCIPLE, WHERE ELEMENTS ARE ADDED AND REMOVED FROM THE TOP. A QUEUE IS A DATA STRUCTURE THAT OPERATES ON THE FIFO (FIRST-IN, FIRST-OUT) PRINCIPLE, WHERE ELEMENTS ARE ADDED TO THE REAR AND REMOVED FROM THE FRONT. 

A REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE OF A STACK IS A SET OF BOOKS ON A SHELF. WHEN YOU PLACE A NEW BOOK ON TOP, YOU MUST REMOVE IT FIRST TO ACCESS THE ONE BELOW. THIS IS SIMILAR TO THE UNDO FUNCTION IN A TEXT EDITOR, WHERE THE MOST RECENT ACTION IS REVERSED FIRST.

A REAL-WORLD EXAMPLE OF A QUEUE IS A LINE OF PEOPLE WAITING AT A BANK. THE FIRST PERSON IN LINE IS SERVED FIRST, FOLLOWED BY THE NEXT PERSON IN LINE. THIS IS SIMILAR TO A PRINTER QUEUE, WHERE PRINT JOBS ARE PROCESSED IN THE ORDER THEY WERE SENT.
